title: Grinding is overrated: the richest people never retire
guest: Jonah Goodhart, co-founder of Mobian (AI contextual classification), serial entrepreneur who sold Moat to Oracle for $850 million, investor in 100+ startups, co-owner of the Surf Lodge in Montauk
summary: A short conference interview with serial entrepreneur Jonah Goodhart followed by the sisters' case-study-style takeaways. Jonah's advice to his 35-year-old self is to 'find your pause' (daily, weekly or sabbatical), to design personal habits for a life of n-of-one, and to pursue the 'happiness quotient' that keeps people like Buffett and Munger working into their 90s. He also reframes advertising as paid storytelling, says AI must serve people, and describes turning down a Lycos acquisition offer as the failure that led to everything since; the hosts discuss pride in early jobs, never retiring, and the difference between distracted rest and true pausing.

ideas.idea: Find your pause: build a daily, weekly or longer break from email, text and social media, because pausing is the only way out of the cycles society pulls you into.
ideas.detail: Jonah's advice to his 35-year-old self; he cites the religious Sabbath as the original model of stepping out of participation for a period, and Jean notes millennials are now baking sabbaticals into career plans.

ideas.idea: Pick habits that are personal to you to design a life of n-of-one; the more your habits come from someone else, the less happy you are.
ideas.detail: Jonah is a big believer in daily habits and says choosing ones that matter to you over time yields more success in life.

ideas.idea: Do every job with pride, even painting a fence and picking up trash at Dairy Queen, because early independence and hard work stay with you.
ideas.detail: Jonah loved earning his own small paycheck at his first job; the hosts add that if you honestly are not proud of your output, you may be in the wrong role for this moment.

ideas.idea: The 'happiness quotient' may matter more for longevity than diet or exercise, so figure out what makes you happy rather than aiming to retire.
ideas.detail: A concept from Jonah's oldest brother: Charlie Munger lived to 99 and Warren Buffett is still working on fast food and soda, while some perfectly fit people die early or are unhappy; the difference is they figured out what drove them.

ideas.idea: If you love your work you never want to retire; the goal is to keep building and teaching into your 80s.
ideas.detail: Cherie points to Stanford GSB professors Glenn Kramon, Joel Peterson and Irv Grousbeck (89 and still teaching, who told her over coffee he will teach 'until I start drooling'); Jean's long-held dream is to retire into a professorship at Dartmouth with a house on Occom Pond.

ideas.idea: Aim to be the coolest 89-year-old with friends of every generation, because staying connected to young people keeps you on the pulse.
ideas.detail: Cherie sets this as a North Star; Jean thinks it is hard without grandchildren or a teaching role since generations rarely mix socially, referencing Imran's point about having a pulse on young people.

ideas.idea: The failure to be most grateful for: turning down a Lycos acquisition in college, watching the company collapse within a year, and having that lead to the companies that followed.
ideas.detail: Jonah and his middle brother, kids on financial aid, thought the company would never stop growing; losing a life-changing offer felt worse than never having it, but it led to a partnership, a second and a third company, ultimately including the $850 million Oracle exit.

ideas.idea: You can only connect the dots looking backwards, so don't sweat apparent mistakes; believe things happen for a reason and keep a positive attitude.
ideas.detail: Jonah cites Steve Jobs's commencement speech; the hosts debate whether this is backward-looking attribution bias but conclude that regret energy is better spent forward-looking, and note humans are naturally loss-minimizing rather than gain-maximizing.

ideas.idea: Advertising is just paid distribution for storytelling, and storytelling is the most foundational concept of humanity.
ideas.detail: Jonah's contrarian take after 26 years in digital advertising and measurement: everyone loves to hate ads, but done well they are inspirational, informative and fun.

ideas.idea: The best conferences are small, invite-only gatherings of intellectually curious, humble people who come to interact, including CEOs of $50-100 billion companies walking around like everyone else.
ideas.detail: Jonah credits Imran's curated event; business, in the end, is about people.

ideas.idea: AI will revolutionize the world, but it exists in service of people; the future is humans plus AI, not humans replaced.
ideas.detail: Humans will still eat, interact and have dreams and goals; AI supports those. Jonah's current company Mobian builds an AI-powered contextual classification engine for internet content.

ideas.idea: Travel somewhere completely different from your world, like Tokyo, as a way to pause and think differently.
ideas.detail: Jonah prefers Tokyo over Aspen or the Hamptons because Japanese society takes honor in daily work, has no trash on the streets, and is successful yet totally different from America.

ideas.idea: The most successful people are humble and never mention their accomplishments; their superpower is making you feel like the only person in the room.
ideas.detail: Jonah never mentioned his $850 million Oracle exit, working with both brothers, or co-owning the Surf Lodge; the sisters spent 90 minutes off camera swapping life stories and describe him as mesmerizing.

ideas.idea: Distracted rest (TV while multitasking) is not pausing; true rest is disconnected, like walks, watercoloring or jewelry making.
ideas.detail: Jean admits her wind-down is Love Island while still working; Cherie suggests trading connected rest for off-Wi-Fi rest, and the sisters consider instituting a weekly day of pause since they currently work every day.
